Brushing Teeth

Toothbrushing often turns into a fight with a clamped-shut mouth and tears. This story turns the two daily minutes into a ritual your child joins willingly.

A personalized picture book in which your child is the hero — and masters this challenge themselves. The first story is free.

Create This Story

Your child's mouth clamps shut, the head twists away, and the moment the brush touches a tooth, out comes "ow, that hurts!" — even though nothing there can actually hurt. Mornings before daycare leave no time for negotiation, evenings everyone is tired, and so two minutes of toothbrushing, twice a day, turns into a small power struggle you never wanted to have. In the end you hold a wriggling child still, brush at top speed to make sure it's actually clean, and you're both irritated before the lights are even out.

Brushing teeth asks something fairly counterintuitive of a small child: allowing a foreign object into their own mouth, even though the mouth is usually the body part most sensitive to anything entering it. Add the taste of toothpaste — the mint that genuinely stings for some children — and the sensation of foam at the back of the throat, which can feel uncomfortably close to gagging. And because a cavity doesn't hurt at first, the child has no immediate experience of why this unpleasant procedure would be worth it at all.

A story puts a face on that abstract necessity: it shows a character who feels exactly the same resistance and still finds a way to make brushing their own thing. Your child isn't hearing a reminder — they're watching someone they identify with master the same hurdle, which often lands harder than any explanation from a parent. And because the story can be read again every evening, your child can follow the same sequence — top, bottom, outside, inside, chewing surfaces — on the page before the brush ever comes out.

In the personalized story, your child brushes their own teeth — their own face on every page — in their own bathroom, guided by a character or a small trick that makes the ritual easier. The story turns the daily resistance into a small, even a genuinely fun moment. The first story is free, so you can try it together before the next brushing battle begins.

Read the book shortly before brushing, not in the middle of an argument about it. A two-minute hourglass or song makes the duration concrete, and a mirror where your child can watch themselves brush adds a sense of control. Until around age six or seven, you should still finish the job afterwards, since fine motor skills for truly thorough brushing develop later — that's normal, not overprotective. If there's persistent pain or noticeable discoloration on the teeth, it's worth booking an appointment with the dentist.

What your child learns

Toothbrushing, oral hygiene, sticking with routines, independence, coping with unpleasant sensations

Recommended age

2-6 years

Frequently Asked Questions

At what age can my child brush their own teeth?

From around age three, your child can actively take part in brushing, but the fine motor skills needed for a truly thorough clean usually don't develop until age six or seven. Until then, let your child brush first and then finish the job yourself.

How often and how long should children's teeth be brushed?

Twice a day, morning and evening, for about two minutes — that's enough to reliably remove plaque. A song or hourglass of that length makes the duration concrete for your child.

What if my child dislikes the taste of toothpaste?

Try a milder children's toothpaste without a strong mint flavor, and let your child pick from two or three options themselves. That small say in the decision often removes a big part of the resistance.

How do I end the daily fight over brushing?

Fixed rituals — always the same order, the same song, the same phrase — give a sense of security. A personalized story where your child, as the main character, brushes their own teeth can reinforce that routine further, since your child already feels familiar with the sequence before the brush comes out.

When should I take my child to the dentist?

The first check-up is usually recommended around the first birthday or once the first teeth come in, and roughly every six months after that, depending on the recommendation. If you notice discoloration, pain, or ongoing refusal to brush, don't put off the appointment.
